title: ⛰️ Avarra — Second Age Political, Social & Cultural Annals
rawNotionMarkup: Avarra • Second Age Years 1–1,437. This is newly developed revisable canon building on the old Ironspine, diverse independent peoples, the Two-Hand Rule, the Eldar Living Calendar, and the later Year 1,322 Southern Wastes catastrophe. Avarran names Awakening, Wonder and Fire are local historical convention. New ancient polities do not automatically become the present Seven Thrones, Aldermere, Valtoria, merchant republics or Eldar High Sovereignty. ## The first generations — the Receding Certainties (Years 1–113) ### The Night of Unlit Steps On several old mountain roads, signal runes that had been reliable over many generations became misleading. In the high valleys, the Night of Unlit Steps refers to a succession of fatal wayfinding accidents when messengers, haulers and rescuers followed glimmering markers toward unsafe ground. It was not one simultaneous magical failure across Eryndor. Khazari stone-carters responded by driving physical stakes into slopes, carving ordinary route marks and maintaining lamp stores that no enchantment was required to light. Some masters gave the work to apprentices, whom they did not always credit; an apprentice named Heska Rellstone became locally renowned for insisting that the people who cleared dangerous roadways deserved the same share of memorial honors as famous runesmiths. In subsequent years some halls adopted a workroll of the living, listing cooks, healers, porters and stone carriers beside engineers. Others refused. This sharpened a wider cultural argument at the roots of the Two-Hand Rule: should a work be admired for its brilliance if ordinary workers were forced to die when it failed? The debate was carried by multiple independent guilds and families, not an edict from a known future Throne. The Ironspine already existed, ancient beyond First Age. ### The River-Stone Breadhouses In a westward river belt, a coalition of grain merchants, Goblin drovers, Human farmers, Halfling growers and some Troll ferry families built the River-Stone Breadhouses: ordinary granaries and ovens maintained with verifiable inventories. They were a pragmatic response to spoiled magically preserved stores. Members contributed food in times of abundance and could seek rations in famine, but there were bitter conflicts over strangers' eligibility. One overseer, Talen Vey, secretly sold emergency flour to creditors; discovery of the theft provoked public hearings and the appointment of rotating stock auditors who did not share a family estate. The reforms succeeded in some communities and failed in others. An elderly Ogre widow remembered as Rhuma of the Low Ford earned renown for ferrying families through floodwater without asking them to present citizenship marks first. Her name survives in folk accounts of different reliability, not an unbroken contemporary archive. ### The woodland grief and the Living Calendar The western woodlands recovered unevenly from altered lunar influences. Some Eldar keepers watched orchards cease flowering on expected nights; others found old groves thriving under the planet's distinct World's Breath. Under Curator Aelthira of the Fern Courts, several forest schools shared seed archives and daylight-based observational records rather than treating rare botanical knowledge as the property of one lineage. A powerful competing circle prohibited seed sharing with outsiders, citing thefts of sacred cuttings and real danger to their forests. Young Eldar, Satyr gardeners, Ent witnesses and Pixie settlements argued over how protection became exclusion. One small archive was deliberately burned during an argument over water access; the new Vow of the Second Copy required a participating school to entrust a duplicate to a neighboring community, ideally one outside its own household. This vow was voluntary and sometimes broken. It was a Second Age innovation, not a surviving First Age record. ## Recovery under imperfect laws (Years 114–321) ### The Court of the Four Weirs A riverine government called the Court of the Four Weirs governed several irrigation basins, toll crossings and towns, with local assemblies only partly represented at its royal court. Its early court was credited with opening floodgates during an ill-timed storm; its later officials began selling rights to the same water. Judge Neral of Northbank, a human law officer whose household was supported by Halfling farmers and Goblin accountants, attempted to make public flood marks admissible evidence against royal water-mages. The court's debate became known as the Argument of Dry Stone: when magic and visible water levels disagree, which may a judge trust? The resulting law required measurement and witnesses in some districts. It did not abolish corruption, and neighboring independent states ignored it. ### The Lantern Refuge and its betrayal A mixed riverside sanctuary founded by Kobold ventilators, Gnome craft teachers, some Brownie households and displaced market families sheltered people unable to pay urban rent. Its rules prohibited forced labor in exchange for immediate rescue. Years later, a council faction began attaching predatory service contracts to admission. the Lantern Petition, carried through market towns by a coalition of children, workers and elders, forced a public accounting and restored shorter terms. Some freed workers never recovered lost years; their survival is part of the history, not proof the settlement was always benevolent. ### Goblin roads and Ogre jurisdictions Goblin communities were not one traveling nation. Some lived permanently in the cities of the Court of Four Weirs, some kept mountain-edge gardens and workshops, and others moved seasonally between distant markets. The Salt-String Caravans carried news of unsafe bridges, suspicious coin and counterfeit warding stones along routes that no kingdom completely controlled. In some provinces, Ogre quarry towns held recognized local courts and trade scales; elsewhere, strong-armed robber bands and human rulers alike exploited isolated roads. The memories of these incidents do not explain later anti-Goblin or anti-Ogre prejudice through Orc wars: there were no Orcs in the Second Age. ## Wonder's opening — power available, but not equally (Years 322–550) ### The Hall of Common Measure At a meeting of otherwise rival Khazari craft houses and Gnomish instrument makers, a demonstration showed how a magnificent new lunar enchantment could hide cracks in an ordinary support beam. They founded the Hall of Common Measure, an experimental meeting place and training network rather than a single mountain kingdom. It offered affordable mechanical inspections alongside magical certification. Foremen liked the reduced risk; enchanted-tool monopolists despised its pricing. Some apprentices forged certificates, causing injuries and scandal. Afterward, the Three-Witness Trial required three independent accounts of a critical test: from a magical practitioner, a physical examiner and a user of the device. That practice spread unevenly. ### A court that starved its own villages A prosperous western lowland principality, the Briar-Crown March, financed monumental enchanted roadways by requiring grain levies from rural districts. The roads were beautiful, shortened trade and enriched urban patrons. During several poor seasons, communities paying the levy went hungry. A coalition of rural tax assessors, Pigfolk bakers, Cowfolk growers, Human fieldworkers and Foxfolk couriers organized the Thousand-Bowl March: an unarmed procession carrying empty bowls to the principality's gate. Guards assaulted protesters and several died. The prince's successor eventually reduced levies and established village appeal hearings, less through charity than fear of further revolt. The roadways' surviving maintenance cost became a byword for splendid projects built on neglected people. ### The forest of divided gifts Several Eldar grove schools developed impressive new moon-fragment arts of growth, light and healing. One made medicine available to nearby settlements at low cost; another restricted it to households that accepted permanent custodianship by the court. Ent councils opposed reckless clearing but were divided on whether intervention against unjust forest lords was their duty. Some Aelwyn Fae offered protection on conditions their neighbors found impossible to understand. No Faerie group is automatically Eldar, Pixie or Brownie. The Open Glade Letters were an agreement among a few woodland teachers to teach basic botanical medicine without demanding a lifetime oath. They did not end secrecy everywhere. ## Wonder's middle centuries — rivalry, reform and memory (Years 551–920) ### The Toll-Bell War (Years 604–607) At three competing waterways west of the old Ironspine, the Briar-Crown March and two self-governing market leagues fought a regional war over tolls and river access. The war included warehouse burnings, short sieges, river skirmishes and deliberate damage to public canals. It did not involve Orcs, the later isolated dark mages or the undated east–west war tradition. A widow's coalition collected the names of missing boatmen across political lines. Their Bell of Returned Names was rung whenever a prisoner or displaced person returned home. The negotiated Greywater Terms limited wartime seizure of grainboats; subsequent rulers sometimes violated them. Hope was not the absence of war, but ordinary people forcing enemies to acknowledge their shared dependents. ### The buried-house debate Among independent Khazari communities the wealthy Stone-Claim Houses argued that the heirs to a discovered abandoned hall could inherit its machinery and secrets. Opponents insisted that spaces full of dangerous devices should be surveyed and made safe before property claims. The argument produced the Seven Lantern Inspections across seven sites—not seven modern Thrones. Some halls were sealed, some reopened, and one excavation was abandoned after fatalities. Their builders and ancient dates remain unknown. This is not evidence the abandoned sites belonged to the First Throne or that Gloin descends from anybody associated with them. ### The years of wandering teachers Gnome lecturers, Merfolk current-watchers from shore markets, Halfling agronomists, Goblin legal clerks and independent Human healers circulated testable instructions that wealthy guilds tried to license. the Roadbook of Errors became a compilation of failed devices, spoiled crops, mislabeled spells and narrow escapes, deliberately recording mistakes alongside successful techniques. Some rulers banned it as an insult to their prestige. Copies survived because traveling families and workshop elders made duplicates. The book was written within the Second Age, not retrieved from the undocumented First. ## Wonder's later years — joy and its price (Years 921–1,321) ### The Nine Hearth Hospitals A group of independent community hospitals, commonly called the Nine Hearth Hospitals, formed across several Avarran market areas; “nine” refers to an early association, not a sacred count of civilizations. Their patrons included rival merchants, women from once-indebted households, healing practitioners and practical supply keepers. Some hospitals offered new lunar-derived healings, but their plain water, food, clean linens and trained care mattered equally. One major patron demanded that debtors be refused aid; a worker coalition threatened to close the hospitals rather than enforce the rule. Their refusal won a limited charter reform and cost several workers their positions. ### Late forests, contested towns Long-lived Eldar witnessed both the Awakening's emergencies and the flourishing of Wonder; some grew confident in protective magic and disliked younger critics who questioned their monopoly over gardens. In the eastern and western lowlands, mixed settlements often succeeded because their markets accepted several peoples' legal practices without requiring identical beliefs. Other towns built walls, excluded outsiders and enforced harsh debt laws. The ability to hide an enchanted settlement did not make its inhabitants universally virtuous or free of internal abuse. ### The southeastern farmland before the Wastes The area that would later become the Southern Wastes was still fertile, lived-in southeastern Avarran farming country through Second Age Year 1,321. Its residents were not knowingly cultivating a natural desert around a pre-existing volcano; the volcano did not yet exist. Regional farm councils, landlords, irrigation workers, family holdings, market hamlets and ordinary religious practices were diverse. Nothing here predetermines the identities or fate of every household in the later catastrophe. Some local records that survive in later copies preserve debates over irrigation and marriage inheritance; no authentic First Age record is hidden among them. ## Avarra during the third era (Years 1,322–1,437) The dark mages were exiled at the beginning of the era, gathered in southeastern Avarra and created both the Southern Wastes and their volcano with dark magic. They did not negotiate alliances, trade or diplomacy with pre-existing outside peoples. The Ashward Flight, Crown of Three Fords and Queen Merea, Hearth-Gate Agreements and Grove-Court of Seralith are established in the separate Era of Fire — Kingdoms, Peoples & Cultural Chronicle (Second Age, 1322–1437). Their political history is not silently backdated into Wonder. At the end of Year 1,437 the world earthquakes amplified by old Ironspine changed far-western Avarra's landscape, magnified volcanic danger, and ended the Second Age. No species went extinct; losses were terrible; the sustaining magical force is still unresolved. ## Inheritance and limits These new chronicles establish particular ancient courts, guilds, movements, wars and family customs but do not imply any modern state was founded in the Second Age. Neither the First Throne's exact dates nor the Silence Below nor Gloin Hammerfeld's ancestry has been settled. The old Ironspine and the newly raised mountains at the western tip are distinct. Modern urban populations and current census totals are not given ancient values. Other continents' era terminology is not imposed by Avarra's historical narrative.
